What it is: The portfolio falls when the market falls.
Likely effect here: Beta of 0.95 against SPY: full equity exposure.
What was done: None by design: no cash, bond or hedging overlay.
How it was checked: Regression in section 6.2; drawdowns in 6.3; falling markets in 8.3.
What remains: High. Inherent in a long-only equity strategy.

What it is: A few very large positions dominate the result.
Likely effect here: About 90 holdings, but the ten largest make up 53% on average; effective number of holdings 26; largest weight reached 13.5%.
What was done: Index rule: at most 9% per stock when the weights are set (reference date). Weights drift above it afterwards.
How it was checked: Section 6.4; variants without limits and with equal weights in 8.1.
What remains: High. The main risk that is specific to this strategy.

Risk or bias: Result driven by few years and few companies
What it is: 93% of the final lead over the index (measured in logs) was earned in the last two of the ten years.
Likely effect here: One dollar in the strategy was worth 2% more than one dollar in SPY at the end of 2023 and 30% more at the end of 2025.
What was done: Nothing: it is a property of the rule in this decade.
How it was checked: Sub-periods and calendar years in sections 6.4 and 8.3; equal-weight variant in 8.1.
What remains: High. Past performance of this kind is not a reliable guide to future performance.

What it is: Past winners lag sharply when market leadership turns, typically in rebounds after a decline.
Likely effect here: Lowers returns in rebound months; worst month of the highest-score against the lowest-score quintile -17.9 pp.
What was done: Long-only and unlevered, so there is no short leg that can lose more than 100%; this limits, but does not remove, the effect.
How it was checked: Worst-month table in section 7; episodes in 8.3.
What remains: High. Leveraged long-short momentum is hit harder, but the long-only version can still lag.

What it is: Large temporary losses that a client must sit through.
Likely effect here: Maximum drawdown -23.1% at month-ends; longest time below a previous peak 26 months.
How it was checked: Section 6.3. Intra-month losses were larger than month-end figures show.

What it is: Winners cluster in sectors; the portfolio becomes a sector bet.
What was done: None: the index rules have no sector limit.

What it is: Orders move prices when they are large relative to trading volume.
Likely effect here: Negligible for a retail account in S&P 500 stocks; relevant for large funds.
How it was checked: Daily dollar volume of the holdings in section 9.2.

Likely effect here: 102% one-way turnover per year, 0.20% cost per year at 10 bp.
What was done: Costs charged on every dollar traded, including the first purchase; two rebalances per year; buffer rule.
How it was checked: Exact cost tests in section 11; sensitivity up to 50 bp in 8.1; break-even cost in 8.2.
What remains: Low to medium. The true cost for a particular broker is unknown.

What it is: Realised short-term gains are taxed every year.
Likely effect here: Would lower after-tax returns relative to a buy-and-hold fund.

What it is: Companies that were later acquired or failed are missing from Yahoo Finance, so the universe is tilted towards survivors.
Likely effect here: Probably overstates stock-portfolio returns by roughly +0.3 pp per year; SPY and SPMO are not affected. Likely flatters the low-score quintiles more than the strategy.
What was done: Point-in-time index membership; reused tickers blocked.
How it was checked: Coverage table (section 3.3); cap-weighted universe against SPY (5.2): +0.36 pp per year; the real fund, which has no such bias, earned 17.9%.
What remains: Medium. Measured at universe level, not removed.

What it is: Using information that was not available on the trade date.
What was done: Every input is dated at least one month before the trade; membership by effective date; risk-free rate lagged; returns start the month after the trade. Three stated exceptions concern share counts (section 2): the unit of a count near a stock split is read with the help of the stock's other counts, later ones included; the count before Yahoo's outage is left out; and a stock's first count is carried back up to 120 days (11% of the weight at the first purchase, at most 0.2% afterwards).
How it was checked: Test that rewrites all future prices and share counts and checks that earlier decisions and values are unchanged (section 11.1); rebuild of every share count used from the counts reported by the reference date (11.2); variants of the share-count rules in 8.1.
What remains: Low for the trading rule. The price-availability filter itself depends on the future (see survivorship).

What it is: Yahoo's share counts are total shares, per company, filed under the ticker of the time, with unit errors near stock splits, a general gap in 2017-18 and a history that starts in 2015.
Likely effect here: Weights differ from the index's float-adjusted weights; some index members cannot be ranked for lack of a share count; a wrong count that Yahoo repeats is accepted.
What was done: Six stated rules (section 2); former tickers of renamed companies mapped (3.1); every unranked member is logged.
How it was checked: Evidence for each rule and largest companies in 3.2; cap-weighted universe against SPY: correlation 0.9994 (5.2); the data variants in 8.1 move the return by at most 0.11 percentage points.

Risk or bias: The backtest is not the index
What it is: Month-end instead of third-Friday trades, total instead of float-adjusted market values, missing companies.
Likely effect here: Before costs the backtest differs from the real fund by +0.15 pp per year on average and by up to +4.7 pp in a single year.
What was done: Every departure from the index rules is listed in section 4.5.
What remains: Medium. The fund's record is the more reliable figure.

What was done: Universe defined by an external rule (index membership at each date), not by the authors.

What it is: Gaps in prices silently change the sample.
What was done: No forward-filling for signals; every exclusion logged with its reason; the engine stops on an unexplained missing return.
How it was checked: Quality gates in section 3.4; exclusion log saved with the outputs.
What remains: Low for the stocks that are in the data.

What it is: Splits, dividends, spin-offs and mergers distort prices if not adjusted.
Likely effect here: Could create false extreme returns and false signals.
What was done: Yahoo's adjusted close for returns, except on 2 days where Yahoo counts a spin-off twice (rule in section 2); ticker changes mapped by hand and documented. The signal uses the close, which is not adjusted for special cash dividends.
How it was checked: Every day with both a split factor and a dividend is listed in section 3; extreme-return table in section 11.
What remains: Low to medium. Spin-offs that Yahoo values wrongly without a double record are not caught.

What it is: The rule's settings (12 months, top fifth, 9% limit, half-yearly) could be lucky choices.
What was done: The settings are those of a published index that was launched before the sample; one-at-a-time sensitivities reported in full.

What it is: Choosing a rule because it did well in the sample, or trying many variants and reporting the best.
Likely effect here: Overstates the evidence: the return shown is in-sample.
What was done: The rule set is a published index's and was not fitted here. It was, however, chosen for this project with knowledge of the sample period. All 22 variants are reported and none is promoted.
How it was checked: Variant log in section 8.1; the fund's live record in 5.2.
What remains: Medium to high. The backtest is not an out-of-sample test, and momentum is one of the most searched patterns in finance.

What it is: Ten years contain few independent market regimes.
Likely effect here: Wide confidence intervals in both directions.
What was done: Block bootstrap; random-portfolio baseline; Monte Carlo with recession regimes.
What remains: High. Not fixable with more computation.
